title: Azure Global Infrastructure: Regions, Availability Zones and Region Pairs (Basic)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain how datacenters, availability zones, regions and geographies fit together, and which kind of failure each level protects you from.
- Compare zonal, zone-redundant and nonzonal (regional) resources, and pick the right behaviour for a web server, a public IP address and a storage account.
- Describe what a region pair gives you, what it does not, and how to plan for a region without a pair such as Indonesia Central.
- Choose a region for a workload by weighing data residency, latency, service and SKU availability, price, availability zones and disaster recovery options.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

The business case from last week landed well. Ibu Sari now asks the practical follow-up: "If we move the shop to Azure, where does it actually live? Jakarta? Singapore? And what happens when that building has a bad day, like our pantry room did when the roof leaked?"

Everyone has an opinion. Dewi wants the closest region because the checkout page feels slow on mobile networks. The finance team has heard that the same service can cost a different amount in another country. Pak Budi points out that the customer database holds names, phone numbers and delivery addresses of Indonesian shoppers, and the legal team would like that data to stay in Indonesia.

You open the list of Azure regions and find dozens of names, zone counts, pairs and footnotes. Before anyone creates a production resource, you need a clear answer for the director: which region should Nusantara Retail use, and how does the shop survive a failure in a building, or in the whole region?

Reading

1. From a building to a geography

Azure is not one giant computer in one place. It is a worldwide fleet of datacenters: buildings full of servers, storage and network equipment, each with its own power feeds, cooling and physical security. You never pick a datacenter directly. Azure groups datacenters into larger units, and you choose among those units instead.

A region is a set of datacenters in one metropolitan area, connected by a fast, low-latency network. When you create a virtual machine, a storage account or a database, you almost always choose a region, and the resource lives there. Each region has a display name for people and a programmatic name for scripts: Indonesia Central is indonesiacentral, Southeast Asia is southeastasia. Microsoft's documentation lists more than 70 regions at the time of writing (October 2026), and new ones keep opening. Indonesia Central, in Jakarta, opened on May 27, 2025.

A geography is a group of one or more regions that forms a data residency boundary, usually a country or a market such as Indonesia, Japan or Europe. Every region belongs to exactly one geography. This detail matters more than it first appears. Southeast Asia (Singapore) and East Asia (Hong Kong) belong to the Asia Pacific geography, while Indonesia Central belongs to the Indonesia geography. If Nusantara Retail must keep customer data inside Indonesia, the geography is the line it may not cross.

A handful of services are nonregional: you don't deploy them into a region at all. Microsoft Entra ID, Azure DNS, Azure Front Door and Azure Traffic Manager run across many regions, so the loss of one region doesn't take them down. Most of what you build in this course is regional, which means the region decision is one you will make again and again.

Two practical notes before we go deeper. First, not every region is open to every customer: a few regions are restricted to specific scenarios, such as in-country disaster recovery, and need an access request. Second, the same service is not necessarily available in every region, and a new region often starts with a smaller catalogue than an established one. Section 5 shows how to check before you commit.

You will see regions in three places. The portal's region dropdown groups them by geography, so Singapore appears as "(Asia Pacific) Southeast Asia". The Azure CLI command az account list-locations returns every region your subscription can see, with its geography, physical location, paired region and zone details. And Microsoft's region list in the documentation shows the same facts for everyone, including regions you can't access yet.

2. Availability zones: separate buildings inside one region

An availability zone is a separate group of one or more datacenters inside a region, with its own independent power, cooling and networking. Zones are placed apart on purpose, typically several kilometres and usually within about 100 kilometres of each other, so a local power cut, fire or flood in one zone should leave the others running. They are also close on purpose: Microsoft aims for round trips between zones of under roughly two milliseconds, which is fast enough to copy data between zones synchronously, before a write is confirmed.

Regions that offer zones have at least three, and a few have more (East US 2 has four at the time of writing). Southeast Asia, East Asia and Indonesia Central each have three. Some regions, mostly older or smaller ones, have no zones at all. And even in a region with zones, an individual service, tier or VM size may not support zones there yet, so always check before you design around them.

Zones protect you from more than disasters. Microsoft aims to roll out platform updates to one zone at a time within a region, so a workload that runs in several zones keeps serving while one zone is being updated. Zones also contain smaller failures, such as a rack or a cluster going down, so the rest of your workload keeps running.

There is one subtlety that surprises almost everyone. When you choose "zone 1", you are choosing a logical zone. Azure maps logical zones to physical zones separately for each subscription, at the moment the subscription is created. Zone 1 in your subscription may therefore be a different building from zone 1 in a colleague's subscription. You can see your own mapping with az account list-locations, which you will do in the lab.

Warning: Never assume that "zone 1" means the same building in two different subscriptions. If you split a workload across subscriptions and care about which physical zone each part lands in, check the logical-to-physical zone mapping for both subscriptions first.

Tip: At the time of writing, Microsoft's availability zone documentation states that Azure doesn't charge for data transfer between availability zones in the same region. Spreading a workload across zones costs you the extra instances, not the traffic between them. Check the current pricing pages before you put this in a business case.

3. Zonal, zone-redundant and nonzonal resources

Having zones in a region doesn't make your resources resilient automatically. What matters is how each resource uses them. Azure services show three behaviours:

- A zonal resource is pinned to one zone that you choose. A virtual machine and its managed disks created with --zone 1 are zonal. A zonal resource is isolated from problems in other zones, but it shares the fate of its own zone: if zone 1 goes dark, so does the VM.
- A zone-redundant resource is spread or replicated across several zones by the service itself. Examples are a Standard public IP created as zone-redundant, a storage account that uses zone-redundant storage (ZRS), the frontend of a Standard load balancer, and databases such as Azure SQL Database or Azure Cosmos DB with zone redundancy turned on. When a zone fails, Microsoft fails over to the remaining zones for you.
- A nonzonal resource, also called a regional resource, is not configured for zones, either because the region has none or because nobody chose any. Azure may place it in any zone and you don't control which one. If that zone has an outage, the resource may go down with it.

Behaviour | Who picks the zone | Survives the loss of one zone? | Examples | Good fit
Zonal | You (zone 1, 2 or 3) | Only if you run copies in other zones yourself | VM, managed disk, zonal public IP | Several VMs spread over zones; very chatty components you want side by side
Zone-redundant | The service, across several zones | Yes, Azure handles the failover | ZRS storage, zone-redundant public IP, load balancer frontend, zone-redundant databases | Shared building blocks that must keep working
Nonzonal (regional) | Nobody; Azure places it | Not guaranteed | Resources created without zone settings; anything in a region without zones | Dev and test, or when another layer handles resilience

Storage makes the difference concrete. Locally redundant storage (LRS) keeps three copies of your data inside a single datacenter: cheap, and fine for data you can rebuild, but a datacenter-wide problem can make all three copies unavailable at once. ZRS writes every change to copies in three or more zones before it confirms the write, so a whole zone can disappear without losing data or availability. Lunch 07 covers all the storage redundancy options.

A design that survives the loss of any single zone is called zone-resilient. You get there in one of two ways: use zone-redundant services, or run several zonal instances in different zones behind something that spreads the traffic, such as a load balancer. The second pattern is exactly how you will protect Nusantara Retail's web servers in Lunch 09.

Two mistakes are worth avoiding from day one. The first is copying a script that says --zone 1 for every VM: you end up with a "highly available" pair of servers that both live in the same zone and fail together. Spread zonal resources deliberately, and remember that a zonal VM keeps its managed disks in the same zone. The second is treating zone redundancy as a backup. ZRS protects you from broken hardware and lost buildings, not from people: if someone deletes or overwrites a file, that change is applied to every copy in every zone within moments. Backups, soft delete and versioning (Lunches 17 and 24) cover that risk.

A closer look at Standard public IPs. Public IPs show why you should read defaults carefully. Basic SKU public IPs were retired on September 30, 2025, so every new public IP is Standard. A Standard public IP can be zonal (created with --zone 1) or zone-redundant (created with --zone 1 2 3). What about one created without any zone setting? In a region with availability zones, Microsoft now treats it as zone-redundant: all former nonzonal Standard IPs in zone-enabled regions were made zone-redundant, and an IP that shows zones 1, 2 and 3 behaves the same as one that shows no zones at all. In a region without zones, every public IP is nonzonal. Two more rules complete the picture: an IP's zone setting can't be changed after creation, and zone-redundant IPs can only be created where three zones are live. In the lab you'll create all three variants and compare their zones property. Writing the zones explicitly in your scripts makes your intent obvious to the next person who reads them.

4. Region pairs, regions without a pair, and sovereign clouds

Zones protect you inside a region. For the rare event that a whole region is lost, Azure has a second idea: region pairs. Microsoft associates some regions with a partner region, usually in the same geography and far enough away that a single disaster is unlikely to hit both. You can't choose your own pair; Microsoft defines it. Southeast Asia and East Asia are a pair.

If your region has a pair and you use that pair as your secondary region, you get some platform benefits, and it pays to be precise about where they stop:

A region pair gives you | A region pair does not give you
Sequential updates: Microsoft staggers planned platform updates across the two regions, so a faulty update is unlikely to hit both at once. | Copies of your VMs, databases or files. Nothing is replicated unless you turn on a feature that does it.
Recovery priority: in a rare geography-wide outage, one region of every pair is prioritised for recovery. | Automatic failover of your workload. You design, build and test that yourself.
Data residency: almost every pair stays inside one geography. Brazil South, paired with South Central US, is the well-known exception. | A choice of partner. The pair is fixed by Microsoft.
A ready-made target for the few services with built-in pair replication, such as geo-redundant storage (GRS). | A guarantee that the services you use support pair-based replication at all.

Important: A region pair is not a backup. Creating a resource in Southeast Asia does not copy it to East Asia. Only features you switch on, such as GRS for a storage account or a geo-replica for a database, move data to another region. Even then, Microsoft-managed failover of GRS accounts happens only in catastrophic situations, so plan and test your own failover whether or not your region has a pair.

Regions without a pair. Many newer regions have no pair at all and rely on availability zones as their main protection. In Asia Pacific these include Indonesia Central, Malaysia West and New Zealand North. "No pair" does not mean "no disaster recovery". It means you choose the second region yourself and set up replication with features that work between any two regions, such as database geo-replicas, storage object replication, Azure Site Recovery for VMs, or backups copied to another region. What disappears are the conveniences that assume a pair: classic geo-redundant storage, for example, replicates to the paired region, so it isn't available where there is no pair. Lunch 17 builds a recovery plan for exactly this situation.

Sovereign clouds. Alongside the global Azure cloud, Microsoft runs separate instances for special legal and regulatory needs: Azure Government for US government agencies and their partners, and Azure operated by 21Vianet in China. They have their own regions, their own sign-in and management endpoints, and often a smaller service catalogue. Nusantara Retail will never need them, but they explain why "Azure" can look different in another market, and why a script written for global Azure may not run there unchanged.

5. Choosing a region for Nusantara Retail

Choosing a region is a design decision, not a default you accept in a dropdown. Work through the same six factors every time, and write the answers down so the next engineer understands why:

Factor | Question to ask | How to check | Nusantara Retail
Data residency and compliance | Must the data stay in a country or a geography? | The region's geography in the region list; your legal or compliance team | Customer data should stay in Indonesia, which points to Indonesia Central
Latency | Where are the users, and how far away is the region? | Test from where your users are; Microsoft also publishes inter-region latency statistics | Shoppers are spread across Indonesia, so Jakarta is the closest region
Service and SKU availability | Does the region offer every service, tier and VM size you need? | The products-by-region page, az provider show and az vm list-skus | Check each service first; Southeast Asia has the broadest catalogue nearby
Price | Does the same thing cost more or less in this region? | The pricing calculator with each candidate region selected | Compare Jakarta and Singapore for the SKUs you will really use
Availability zones | Can you spread the workload across zones? | The region list, and the zone mapping in the CLI | Both regions have three zones
Disaster recovery options | Is there a pair, and which second region could you use? | The region pairs list and each service's reliability guide | Indonesia Central has no pair, so the plan is your own

Distances matter for that last row. In Microsoft's published round-trip statistics between regions (median values for the 30 days ending July 30, 2026), Indonesia Central and Southeast Asia are about 16 to 17 milliseconds apart, while Indonesia Central to East Asia is about 47 milliseconds. Those numbers describe traffic inside Microsoft's network; what a shopper in Makassar experiences also depends on their mobile provider, which is why you should measure from where your users really are.

Price deserves the same care. A small difference per hour turns into a real amount for servers that run all month, and a second region adds more than its own resources: replication traffic between regions appears on the bill as data transfer. Price the whole design in the pricing calculator, including the recovery region, before you promise Ibu Sari a number.

For Nusantara Retail the answer is taking shape. Production runs in Indonesia Central, spread across its three zones: zone-redundant services wherever they exist, and several zonal VMs where the design needs VMs. Backups stay in the region. Whether a second copy may live outside Indonesia, with Southeast Asia as the obvious candidate, is a question for the legal team, not for you alone. Meanwhile the labs use Southeast Asia, because it has three zones, a pair and the broadest service catalogue nearby; you can switch any lab to indonesiacentral by setting LOCATION.

Pause and think: Ibu Sari asks, "If the whole Jakarta region went down, would we lose customer data?" With the plan above, what is your honest answer, and which single decision would change it?

In the next lunch you look one level up from the region: how subscriptions, resource groups and Azure Resource Manager organise everything you create, wherever it lives.

Field notes from Stefanus

Name the failure before you pick the region. Before anyone opens the region dropdown, I ask one question: which failure must this design survive — a rack, a building or a whole region? Then every box on the architecture diagram gets a label: zonal, zone-redundant or nonzonal. Unlabelled boxes are where the surprises hide, typically a "highly available" pair of VMs that were both created with --zone 1. At the region level my rule is just as short: if nobody can name the feature that copies the data to another region, there is no copy, pair or no pair. And I measure latency from a phone on the kind of mobile network the users really have, never only from Cloud Shell: it runs inside an Azure datacenter, so it can't tell me what a shopper feels.

Go further

- What are Azure regions? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/reliability/regions-overview) — geographies, regions, nonregional services and the factors Microsoft suggests for choosing regions.
- What are availability zones? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview) — zonal and zone-redundant support, logical and physical zones, and the current list of regions with zones.
- Azure region pairs and nonpaired regions (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/reliability/regions-paired) — the full pair list, the asymmetric exceptions and the regions that have no pair.
- Azure network round-trip latency statistics (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/networking/azure-network-latency) — median latency between Azure regions, useful when you pick a recovery region.

quiz.q: Dewi creates the only web server with --zone 2 and nothing in any other zone. Zone 2 then loses power. What happens to the shop, and what is the name for this kind of resource?
quiz.a: The VM is zonal, so it goes down with zone 2 and the shop is offline until the zone recovers. Why: a zonal resource shares the fate of its zone; to survive, run a second VM in another zone behind a load balancer.

quiz.q: Product photos are stored in Southeast Asia with zone-redundant storage (ZRS). Are they protected if the entire Southeast Asia region becomes unavailable?
quiz.a: No. ZRS keeps copies in several zones of one region; a region-wide outage needs a copy in another region, for example geo-zone-redundant storage to East Asia or your own replication. Why: zones protect against the loss of a zone, not of a whole region.

quiz.q: A colleague says: "We're in Southeast Asia, which is paired with East Asia, so our VMs fail over to Hong Kong automatically." Is that right?
quiz.a: No. A pair gives sequential updates, recovery priority and data residency, but it never copies or fails over your VMs; you would need something like Azure Site Recovery and a tested plan. Why: only features you turn on use the pair.

quiz.q: The legal team decides that customer data must stay in Indonesia. Which region do you choose, and what does disaster recovery look like?
quiz.a: Indonesia Central, spread across its three zones, with backups kept in the region; any copy to another region, such as Southeast Asia, would leave Indonesia, so it needs the legal team's approval. Why: the region has no pair, and the geography is the data residency boundary.

quiz.q: You create a Standard public IP in Southeast Asia without any zone setting, and az network public-ip show lists no zones. Is the IP zonal, zone-redundant or nonzonal?
quiz.a: Zone-redundant. In regions with availability zones, Standard public IPs created without zones are treated as zone-redundant; only in a region without zones would it be nonzonal. Why: Microsoft made all former nonzonal Standard IPs zone-redundant, so set zones explicitly when you want to make your intent visible.

takeaways: A geography is a data residency boundary, a region is a set of datacenters in one metro area, and an availability zone is a separate group of datacenters with its own power, cooling and network.
Zones only help if your resources use them: zonal resources share their zone's fate, zone-redundant resources survive a zone failure, and nonzonal resources give no guarantee.
Region pairs bring sequential updates, recovery priority and data residency, but never automatic replication or failover of your workloads.
Regions without a pair, such as Indonesia Central, rely on zones; for regional disasters you choose your own second region and set up replication, if your data rules allow it.
Choose a region on residency, latency, service and SKU availability, price, zones and DR options, and verify each one with the documentation or the CLI before you build.

lab.title: Explore regions and zones
lab.text:
What you'll build

Before Nusantara Retail commits to a region, Ibu Sari wants evidence, not opinions. In this lab you collect it. You use the Azure CLI to list regions, their geographies and pairs, read your subscription's logical-to-physical zone mapping and check which VM sizes and services are offered where. Then you build small, cheap resources that make the difference between zonal and zone-redundant visible: three Standard public IPs (zonal, zone-redundant and "no zone given") and two storage accounts (LRS and ZRS). You finish with a short latency check from your own browser.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/03-global-infrastructure
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 03)
ST_LRS="stnusalrs${SUFFIX}"
ST_ZRS="stnusazrs${SUFFIX}"

- This lab has no setup.sh: you create everything yourself.
- LOCATION must be a region with availability zones. The default, southeastasia, has three. Learners in Indonesia can run export LOCATION=indonesiacentral and then source ../common/config.sh again; it also has three zones.
- If Cloud Shell times out and restarts, cd back into the lab folder and run the four lines after cd again.

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Standard public IPv4 addresses are billed by the hour even when nothing uses them. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–5 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Regions, geographies and pairs

Every region belongs to a geography (a data residency boundary), and some regions have a paired region. The CLI shows exactly what your subscription can see, so start there.

# How many physical regions can your subscription see?
az account list-locations --query "length([?metadata.regionType=='Physical'])"

# The regions closest to Nusantara Retail: geography, city and paired region
az account list-locations \
  --query "[?contains(['indonesiacentral','southeastasia','eastasia','malaysiawest'], name)].{region:name, geography:metadata.geography, city:metadata.physicalLocation, pair:metadata.pairedRegion[0].name}" \
  --output table

# Which physical regions have no paired region at all?
az account list-locations \
  --query "[?metadata.regionType=='Physical' && !metadata.pairedRegion].displayName" \
  --output tsv | sort

The first command counts only physical regions. The list also contains logical entries such as "Asia Pacific", which group regions for some services and are not places you deploy to.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open the region dropdown on any Create page (for example Create a resource group): regions are grouped by geography, such as "(Asia Pacific) Southeast Asia". The pairs and zone counts are easier to read in Microsoft's list of Azure regions (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/reliability/regions-list).

Checkpoint: the table shows eastasia as the pair of southeastasia (and the other way round), while indonesiacentral and malaysiawest show an empty pair column. Indonesia Central appears in the "no pair" list. The geography column shows the Singapore and Hong Kong regions in one geography and Jakarta in another (the exact wording comes from the platform and can differ slightly from the documentation).

Task 2 · Look inside your region: zones, zone mapping and what's offered

Zones are numbered 1, 2 and 3 in every subscription, but the numbers are logical. Each subscription has its own mapping to the physical zones, and you can read yours.

# Your subscription's logical-to-physical zone mapping for LOCATION
az account list-locations \
  --query "[?name=='${LOCATION}'].availabilityZoneMappings | [0]" \
  --output table

# How many regions offer zones to your subscription?
az account list-locations --query "length([?availabilityZoneMappings])"

Next, check which VM sizes your subscription can deploy into zones. The SKU list is big, so this command can take a minute or two; read the next paragraph while you wait.

az vm list-skus --location "$LOCATION" --resource-type virtualMachines \
  --size Standard_B --zone --output table

--zone keeps only sizes that support availability zones, and the Zones column shows which zones each size is offered in. By default the list hides sizes that are restricted for your subscription; add --all to see them too, with the reason in the Restrictions column.

Finally, ask Azure Resource Manager whether a service is offered in a region. Every resource provider publishes the locations of each resource type:

for rt in Microsoft.Network/natGateways Microsoft.App/managedEnvironments; do
  ns="${rt%%/*}"; type="${rt#*/}"
  echo "== ${rt}"
  az provider show --namespace "$ns" \
    --query "resourceTypes[?resourceType=='${type}'].locations | [0]" --output tsv \
    | grep -i -E "indonesia|southeast asia|east asia" || echo "   (not listed in these regions)"
done

Tip: Prefer the portal? The public products available by region page answers the same question for every product. The CLI is better for exact resource types, sizes and your own subscription's restrictions.

Checkpoint: the mapping table shows three rows (logical zones 1, 2 and 3, each with a physical zone name such as southeastasia-az2); your logical 1 is not necessarily physical 1. The SKU table lists several B-series sizes with 1,2,3 in the Zones column. The loop prints the region names where each resource type is offered.

Task 3 · Zonal, zone-redundant and "no zone" public IPs

Public IPs are a perfect test object: they are created in seconds, cost very little, and their zone setting is visible. Create the resource group and three Standard public IPv4 addresses.

ensure_rg "$RG" 03

# Zonal: pinned to logical zone 1
az network public-ip create --resource-group "$RG" --name pip-nusa-zonal \
  --location "$LOCATION" --sku Standard --version IPv4 --allocation-method Static \
  --zone 1 --output none

# Zone-redundant: spread across zones 1, 2 and 3
az network public-ip create --resource-group "$RG" --name pip-nusa-zr \
  --location "$LOCATION" --sku Standard --version IPv4 --allocation-method Static \
  --zone 1 2 3 --output none

# No zone given: what does Azure do?
az network public-ip create --resource-group "$RG" --name pip-nusa-nozone \
  --location "$LOCATION" --sku Standard --version IPv4 --allocation-method Static \
  --output none

Now compare them:

az network public-ip list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{name:name, sku:sku.name, allocation:publicIPAllocationMethod, zones:join(', ', zones || \`[]\`)}" \
  --output table

How to read the result:

- pip-nusa-zonal shows 1. It is zonal: it lives in zone 1 and shares that zone's fate.
- pip-nusa-zr shows 1, 2, 3. It is zone-redundant: it survives the loss of any single zone.
- pip-nusa-nozone most likely shows an empty zones column. Don't read that as "nonzonal". In a region with availability zones, Microsoft treats a Standard public IP without a zone setting as zone-redundant; an IP that shows no zones behaves the same as one that shows 1, 2, 3. Only in a region without zones is a public IP truly nonzonal. Depending on the API version, the field might also come back filled in. Either way, set --zone explicitly in your scripts so that your intent is clear to the next reader.

One more rule: the zone setting of a public IP is fixed at creation. To change it, you create a new IP, which also means a new address, so decide before you hand the address to a partner or a DNS record.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › Public IP addresses › Create: look at the Availability zone setting and the options it offers in your region, then leave the page without creating anything.

Checkpoint: three Standard, Static IPs exist in rg-lunch03-<suffix>, with zones 1, 1, 2, 3 and (most likely) nothing.

Task 4 · LRS versus ZRS storage

Storage accounts make the same choice visible as redundancy. Locally redundant storage (LRS) keeps three copies in one datacenter; zone-redundant storage (ZRS) keeps copies in three zones and confirms a write only after every copy has it. Create one of each, both with TLS 1.2 as the minimum and anonymous blob access turned off.

az storage account create --name "$ST_LRS" --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 --min-tls-version TLS1_2 --allow-blob-public-access false \
  --output none

az storage account create --name "$ST_ZRS" --resource-group "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --sku Standard_ZRS --kind StorageV2 --min-tls-version TLS1_2 --allow-blob-public-access false \
  --output none

Compare them:

az storage account list --resource-group "$RG" \
  --query "[].{name:name, sku:sku.name, primary:primaryLocation, secondary:secondaryLocation, status:statusOfPrimary}" \
  --output table

Both accounts live in your LOCATION and the secondary column is empty for both: LRS and ZRS never leave the region. ZRS protects you from losing a datacenter or a whole zone; it doesn't protect you from losing the region, and, like every redundancy option, it copies deletions and overwrites too. A secondary location only appears with the geo-redundant options (GRS, GZRS), which replicate to the paired region. The stretch goals let you see that.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › Storage accounts › Create: the Redundancy dropdown on the Basics tab offers the same choices. Compare what it offers in Southeast Asia and in Indonesia Central.

Checkpoint: two StorageV2 accounts, stnusalrs<suffix> with Standard_LRS and stnusazrs<suffix> with Standard_ZRS, both with your LOCATION as primary and no secondary.

Task 5 (optional) · A rough latency check from your browser

Cloud Shell runs inside an Azure datacenter, so it can't tell you what your shoppers feel. Your own browser can.

1. Open the community-built Azure Latency Test page (a free third-party tool, not a Microsoft service).
2. Select Indonesia Central, Southeast Asia, East Asia and Malaysia West, and let it run for a minute.
3. Note the median round trip for each region and compare.

Treat the numbers as a rough signal: the test runs over HTTPS from your browser, so DNS lookups and TLS handshakes are included, and the result depends on your own internet provider. For region-to-region numbers measured inside Microsoft's network, use Microsoft's inter-region latency statistics (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/networking/azure-network-latency).

Checkpoint: you have four latency figures. From most places in Indonesia you would expect Jakarta to be the fastest, but your network has the final word. That's exactly why you measure.

Break it and fix it

Zone-redundant storage needs a region with availability zones. Try to create a ZRS account in a region that has none.

# Find a physical region without availability zones (falls back to westus, which has none)
NOZONE_REGION=$(az account list-locations \
  --query "[?metadata.regionType=='Physical' && metadata.regionCategory=='Recommended' && !availabilityZoneMappings].name | [0]" \
  --output tsv)
NOZONE_REGION=${NOZONE_REGION:-westus}
echo "Region without zones: ${NOZONE_REGION}"

az storage account create --name "stnusabrk${SUFFIX}" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --location "$NOZONE_REGION" --sku Standard_ZRS --kind StorageV2 --output none

Symptom: the command fails with an error saying that the Standard_ZRS SKU isn't supported or available in that location. (If the error says instead that the location isn't available for your subscription, pick another region from the list and try again.)

Hint and fix

ZRS spreads copies across availability zones, so it only exists where zones exist. Before you choose a redundancy option, check the region:

az account list-locations --query "[?name=='${NOZONE_REGION}'].availabilityZoneMappings | [0]" --output table

An empty result means no zones. Fix it by choosing a zone-enabled region (--location "$LOCATION") or, if you really need that region, by using Standard_LRS and accepting that a datacenter failure takes the data offline. Then make sure nothing extra was created:

if az storage account show --name "stnusabrk${SUFFIX}" --resource-group "$RG" --output none 2>/dev/null; then
  az storage account delete --name "stnusabrk${SUFFIX}" --resource-group "$RG" --yes
else
  echo "Nothing to remove: the failed request created nothing."
fi

This deletes everything the lab created: the resource group rg-lunch03-<suffix> with its public IPs and storage accounts. Nothing in this lab lives outside the resource group. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
az vm list-skus prints nothing for a long time | It downloads the whole SKU catalogue for the region before printing | Wait up to two minutes; keep --size to narrow the output
Zone mapping table is empty | LOCATION points to a region without availability zones (or a typo) | Run echo $LOCATION; use southeastasia or indonesiacentral
(StorageAccountAlreadyTaken) The storage account named ... is already taken. | Storage account names are global and someone else has yours | Run bash cleanup.sh, then rm ~/.azlunches-suffix, source ../common/config.sh again (new suffix) and repeat Tasks 3–4
Public IP creation fails with an error about zones | The region has no zones, or not all three zones are live there | Use a zone-enabled region for LOCATION
(MissingSubscriptionRegistration) The subscription is not registered to use namespace 'Microsoft.Network' | A brand-new subscription hasn't used that resource provider yet | az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Network, wait a minute, retry
pip-nusa-nozone shows an empty zones column | Expected: in a zone-enabled region it is zone-redundant anyway | Re-read the explanation in Task 3
verify.sh says the resource group is missing after you changed LOCATION | The suffix or region in this shell differs from when you created things | source ../common/config.sh with the same LOCATION you used before
